case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal district courts may issue injunctions that bar the Executive Branch from enforcing a challenged presidential policy against anyone nationwide (i.e., beyond the parties) when the plaintiffs have established injury only to themselves.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing and judicial power) and equitable remedial principles governing injunctions; underlying merits implicate the Fourteenth Amendment Citizenship Clause ("All persons born ... in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens"), though the Government seeks narrowing without merits review.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Government (Trump, et al.) argues it is likely to succeed on the claim that the district courts’ injunctions are overbroad because universal/nationwide injunctions exceed Article III limits and traditional equity by extending relief to nonparties, create asymmetric enforcement burdens (the government must win everywhere before enforcing anywhere), interfere with internal executive operations, and improperly give plaintiffs the functional benefits of class-wide relief without meeting Rule 23 requirements; the Court can narrow the injunctions on stay without reaching the underlying constitutionality of the challenged order.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (CASA and aligned state/organizational parties) argue broader relief is necessary to provide complete relief and to prevent ongoing enforcement of unlawful/unconstitutional executive action, that universal remedies are not categorically barred by Article III or equity (and are consistent with how courts handle invalid government action), that channeling challenges into Rule 23 would not solve the government’s asserted problems (including inter-circuit "asymmetry"), and that using this emergency posture to restrict remedial power while assuming the policy’s illegality would dangerously weaken the judiciary; on the merits backdrop, amici for respondents contend birthright citizenship is well supported by precedent and history, while other amici dispute that reading of Wong Kim Ark.
key_precedents: United States v. Wong Kim Ark, 169 U.S. 649 (1898)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: when the Government applies a uniform policy, party-only relief can be practically “illusory” because the same regime may re-injure plaintiffs through ongoing enforcement and third-party interactions. But under our remedial precedents (Madsen; Califano) and the caution in Grupo Mexicano—emphasized by Justice Kagan—equity’s breadth still tracks necessity to afford complete relief to the parties before the court, and respondents have not shown that plaintiff-specific (or properly certified class) relief cannot fully remedy these plaintiffs as a legal matter rather than merely as a matter of administrative convenience. Sullivan v. Zebley, as Justice Thomas notes, illustrates that broad operational consequences can follow when needed to cure the plaintiffs’ injuries in a representative posture; it does not supply a freestanding Article III license for a universal injunction protecting nonparties by default. In this emergency posture, a narrow disposition that stays or narrows the injunctions to the plaintiffs (and any certified class) best preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids unnecessary merits pronouncements on the Citizenship Clause.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s “illusory relief” point has intuitive appeal, but under an originalist and textualist view it cannot expand Article III’s case-or-controversy power into authority to control the Government’s conduct toward nonparties simply because the Executive acts uniformly. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, our remedial precedents (e.g., Madsen and Califano) require injunctions to be no more burdensome than necessary to afford complete relief to the plaintiffs, and “uniformity” is a policy consideration, not a jurisdictional grant. Sullivan v. Zebley, invoked by the respondents, does not supply historical grounding for universal injunctions; its broad operational effect followed from providing complete relief in a representative (class) posture, not a freestanding decree protecting strangers nationwide. Grupo Mexicano (as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize) reinforces that we should not innovate new forms of equity untethered to traditional practice, and on a stay posture the proper course is narrowing relief to the parties (or a certified class) without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: that a uniform federal policy can make party-limited relief practically ineffective and invite recurring harm through third-party interactions, and they cite Sullivan v. Zebley. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains through Madsen and Califano, equity’s touchstone is tailoring—an injunction should be no more burdensome than necessary to provide complete relief to the plaintiffs—and “uniformity” cannot itself expand Article III power to regulate the Government’s conduct toward nonparties. Zebley does not change that conclusion because its broad operational effects were tied to providing full relief in a representative posture (classwide features), not a freestanding license for a single district judge to impose nationwide rules absent Rule 23 safeguards or a concrete showing that plaintiff-specific relief cannot make these plaintiffs whole. In this stay posture, narrowing the injunction to the parties (or a properly certified class) respects traditional equitable limits (Grupo Mexicano) without deciding the Citizenship Clause merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize Madsen/Califano tailoring and Grupo Mexicano’s caution against freewheeling equity, and their point strengthens the demand that any broad decree be justified as necessary to secure complete relief rather than as a general “uniformity” preference. But I do not accept that those limits translate into a near-categorical parties-only rule on a stay posture when the challenged federal regime is administered uniformly and predictably re-injures the same plaintiffs through ongoing enforcement and third-party interactions; in that setting, "complete relief" can require operationally broader prohibitions to prevent immediate recurrence of the constitutional harm. Justice Thomas’s historical critique underscores the institutional costs of universal injunctions, yet it does not establish an Article III bar where broader relief is functionally required to protect the plaintiffs from continuing injury pending merits review, and Sullivan v. Zebley remains a concrete example that systemwide remedies can be a permissible incident of making the challengers whole. Rule 23 is often preferable, but equity should not be artificially cramped in a way that leaves vulnerable newborns and families exposed to predictable enforcement churn before we can resolve the merits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is functional: in a uniform federal regime, party-only relief can be “illusory” because third-party interactions and ongoing enforcement may predictably re-inflict the same injury. But as Chief Justice Roberts frames it under Madsen/Califano, that practical concern still has to be cashed out as a necessity-to-make-these-plaintiffs-whole showing, not a generalized uniformity rationale for regulating the Government’s conduct toward nonparties; otherwise we effectively bypass Rule 23’s legitimacy and administrability safeguards. Sullivan v. Zebley does matter, yet it fits more naturally as an example where broad operational consequences flowed from providing complete relief in a representative/class posture, not as authority for a freestanding universal injunction untethered to party-based redress. On this stay posture, narrowing to plaintiffs (and any certified class) respects Article III and traditional equitable limits (Grupo Mexicano) while leaving room for broader relief if a concrete evidentiary showing demonstrates that narrower protection truly cannot prevent likely re-injury to these plaintiffs.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is her functional account of “complete relief” under a uniform federal policy, but under Article III and traditional equity that concept remains tethered to redressing the plaintiffs’ own injuries—not ensuring nationwide uniformity for all similarly situated nonparties. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, our tailoring cases (Madsen; Califano) and Grupo Mexicano’s history-bound approach counsel against treating universal injunctions as the default absent a representative mechanism; Sullivan v. Zebley does not establish a freestanding power to protect strangers to the suit, but rather reflects relief necessary to remedy the injuries of plaintiffs in a posture with representative features. If respondents can show that party-specific relief truly cannot prevent likely re-injury to these plaintiffs (as opposed to being less convenient), equity can account for that; but on this stay posture, the asserted “illusory” nature of narrower relief sounds in policy and administration, not judicial power. Accordingly, I would narrow the injunction to the parties (and any properly certified class) without resolving the Citizenship Clause merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson persuasively stress that parties-only relief can be practically “illusory” under a uniformly administered federal policy, but that functional concern cannot itself supply Article III authority to regulate the Government’s conduct toward nonparties. As Chief Justice Roberts explains via Madsen and Califano, the remedial touchstone is tailoring—no more burdensome than necessary to afford complete relief to the plaintiffs—and respondents have not shown that protecting these plaintiffs (or any properly certified class) is inadequate to redress their injuries as opposed to merely less convenient for nationwide uniformity. Sullivan v. Zebley, invoked by Sotomayor and Jackson, reinforces that broader relief may sometimes be necessary to make the plaintiffs whole in a systemic program challenge, yet it does not establish a freestanding power to issue universal injunctions absent a representative posture or a demonstrated necessity tied to these plaintiffs’ risk of re-injury. Given the emergency posture and institutional costs Thomas and Gorsuch highlight, the modest, historically grounded course is to narrow the injunctions without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point—that parties-only relief can be “illusory” when a uniform federal policy predictably re-injures plaintiffs—identifies a real practical concern, but under an originalist and textualist view it cannot by itself expand Article III power beyond redressing the plaintiffs’ injuries. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, our tailoring cases (Madsen; Califano) require an injunction to be no more burdensome than necessary to provide complete relief, and respondents have not shown that protecting these plaintiffs (or a properly certified class) is inadequate rather than merely less convenient for national uniformity. Sullivan v. Zebley does not alter that conclusion because its broad operational effect was tethered to relief for a certified class challenging administration of a federal benefits scheme, not a freestanding judicial authority to regulate the Government’s dealings with all nonparties. Given Grupo Mexicano’s caution against expanding equity beyond traditional bounds, especially on a stay posture, narrowing the injunctions is the institutionally modest course without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s tailoring principle (Madsen/Califano) is the hardest objection, and I agree it should do real work: an injunction must be no more burdensome than necessary to provide complete relief. But their response assumes—without grappling with the operational record—that party-only relief is actually “complete” when a single uniform citizenship policy predictably re-injures the same plaintiffs through ongoing nationwide enforcement and third-party reliance; if the Government’s system continues to treat the plaintiffs as noncitizens in interconnected federal and state interactions, narrower relief can become administratively illusory. Justice Thomas’s Grupo Mexicano point properly cautions against free-floating “universal” equity, yet it does not answer the more modest proposition that equity may sometimes require broader operational constraints to stop recurrent harm to the parties from an unlawful, uniformly administered regime (Sullivan v. Zebley illustrates that consequence), especially on a stay posture where the risk of churn and unequal treatment is immediate. Rule 23 is often preferable, but I am not persuaded that equitable power must be categorically withheld absent class certification when narrower relief cannot realistically prevent continuing injury to the plaintiffs themselves.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III confines the judicial power to resolving the parties’ case or controversy, and equitable relief must be tailored to redress the plaintiffs’ proven injury rather than to regulate the rights of nonparties. This Court has repeatedly emphasized that an injunction “should be no more burdensome to the defendant than necessary to provide complete relief to the plaintiffs,” Madsen v. Women’s Health Ctr., Inc., 512 U.S. 753, 765 (1994), a principle echoed in Califano v. Yamasaki, 442 U.S. 682, 702 (1979), and consistent with standing limits described in Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490, 499 (1975). Where plaintiffs show only individualized injury, extending relief to strangers to the suit risks exceeding the traditional bounds of equity and undermines institutional legitimacy by forcing the Executive to prevail everywhere before acting anywhere. The injunctions should therefore be narrowed to the parties (or to properly certified classes) without reaching the underlying Citizenship Clause merits in this emergency posture.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III confines the “judicial Power” to resolving concrete “Cases” and “Controversies,” which requires remedies to be tailored to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries rather than to regulate the Executive’s conduct toward nonparties nationwide. Traditional equitable principles likewise demanded relief no broader than necessary to provide complete relief to the parties, and a district court’s universal injunction—functionally granting classwide relief without satisfying Rule 23—exceeds those limits and distorts the separation of powers by forcing the Government to prevail everywhere before enforcing anywhere. While the merits may implicate the Fourteenth Amendment Citizenship Clause, the Government is entitled on a stay posture to narrowing relief to the parties without prejudging constitutionality. As I explained in Trump v. Hawaii, universal injunctions lack grounding in the original understanding of Article III equity and should be rejected absent clear constitutional or statutory authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III confines the federal courts to resolving the parties’ concrete disputes, and equitable relief must be no broader than necessary to remedy the plaintiffs’ own injury; an injunction that categorically bars enforcement against nonparties exceeds that traditional limitation and risks converting a single case into de facto nationwide policymaking. Our remedial precedents emphasize tailoring: in Califano v. Yamasaki, 442 U.S. 682 (1979), the Court explained that injunctions should be limited to the extent necessary to provide complete relief to the plaintiffs, not to regulate the Government’s conduct toward everyone. Allowing universal injunctions also produces serious practical consequences—encouraging forum shopping, imposing asymmetric nationwide enforcement constraints on the Executive, and bypassing Rule 23’s safeguards for representative litigation—without any showing that narrower, party-focused relief would be inadequate here. In this emergency posture, the Court can and should narrow the injunctions to the plaintiffs (and any properly certified class) without reaching the merits of the underlying Citizenship Clause dispute under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires a plaintiff to establish injury-in-fact, but once jurisdiction is established, equitable relief may extend as far as necessary to afford complete relief and prevent ongoing harm from an unlawful federal policy; limiting an injunction to named parties can be illusory where a single federal rule is applied uniformly and the injury would recur through third-party interactions and constant enforcement churn. Traditional equitable principles permit tailoring relief to the practical realities of nationwide administration, and this Court has long recognized that when a federal policy is unlawful, courts may order broad remedial relief adequate to cure the violation rather than a patchwork remedy that leaves vulnerable people exposed to continued enforcement. Sullivan v. Zebley illustrates that sweeping relief against an invalid federal regime is sometimes required to secure meaningful protection and that the Government’s “asymmetry” concerns can persist even with classwide relief, undermining the claim that narrowing injunctions is compelled by Article III. Given the grave constitutional backdrop of the Fourteenth Amendment Citizenship Clause and the need for uniformity in citizenship status, I would not, on an emergency stay posture, cut back remedial authority in a way that predictably denies effective relief to those most at risk.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III limits federal courts to resolving the parties’ cases and controversies, and equitable relief must be tailored to providing complete relief to the plaintiffs rather than operating as a generally applicable “nationwide” veto on Executive enforcement against nonparties. Under Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo v. Alliance Bond Fund, federal equitable power is bounded by traditional practice, and the modern “universal injunction” is at least in tension with that history unless justified as necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries. Respondents’ reliance on the asserted illegality of the policy and the desirability of uniformity cannot substitute for Rule 23 mechanisms when relief is effectively classwide, and broad injunctions risk the workability problems the Government identifies (asymmetric nationwide lock-in from a single district). Without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits (Wong Kim Ark), the proper course is to narrow relief to the plaintiffs and those similarly situated only if properly certified or otherwise necessary to afford complete relief.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III empowers federal courts to resolve "Cases" and "Controversies" by redressing the plaintiffs’ own injuries, and traditional equitable principles require injunctions to be no broader than necessary to afford complete relief to the parties before the court. Universal injunctions that forbid enforcement against nonparties effectively confer classwide relief without satisfying Rule 23’s procedural safeguards, and they risk upsetting the separation of powers by allowing a single district judge to dictate nationwide Executive Branch policy based on one case. While some historical equity devices (e.g., bills of peace) could bind or protect nonparties, they did so through representative procedures and identifiable groups, not by issuing freestanding, nationwide decrees untethered to the parties’ proven injuries. Consistent with Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., 527 U.S. 308 (1999), federal equitable power should not be expanded beyond the traditional bounds absent clear congressional authorization, so the injunctions should be narrowed without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III limits the federal courts to resolving the cases and controversies of the parties before them, and traditional equitable principles generally require tailoring injunctive relief to remedy the plaintiffs’ own injury rather than regulating the Executive’s conduct toward nonparties. Even assuming serious merits questions under the Fourteenth Amendment Citizenship Clause and cases like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, the proper course in this posture is to narrow relief to what is necessary to provide complete relief to these plaintiffs, leaving broader, nonparty protection to mechanisms like class certification under Rule 23 or to higher-court resolution. The Court has cautioned that injunctions should be no broader than necessary to provide complete relief, and universal injunctions create practical and institutional problems by forcing the Government to win everywhere before it can enforce anywhere and by encouraging forum shopping. In light of those Article III and equity constraints and the Court’s preference for workability and restrained remedies, the district courts exceeded their authority in imposing nationwide relief on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III limits the judicial power to resolving the case or controversy before the court, and equitable relief must be tailored to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries rather than confer freestanding protection on nonparties nationwide. Under Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo v. Alliance Bond Fund, federal courts’ equitable authority is constrained by traditional equitable principles and should not be expanded to new, broadly prophylactic forms absent clear historical grounding or legislative authorization. Whatever the merits backdrop under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and Wong Kim Ark, the Government may obtain narrowing on stay because the district courts’ universal injunctions appear to exceed what is necessary to afford complete relief to these plaintiffs and effectively bypass Rule 23’s requirements for binding, classwide relief. Precedent does not foreclose injunctions with incidental third-party effects, but it does not support nationwide relief untethered from the plaintiffs’ injuries as a default remedy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III limits courts to resolving cases and controversies and tailoring remedies to redress plaintiffs’ injuries, but equitable principles also require relief that is practically sufficient to prevent ongoing harm from an unlawful federal policy—especially where partial relief would be administratively unworkable or would predictably re-inflict the same injury through nationwide enforcement. In the government-policy context, this Court has affirmed broad injunctive relief where needed to afford complete relief against unlawful rules, as in Sullivan v. Zebley, 493 U.S. 521 (1990), which sustained relief with nationwide operational consequences rather than forcing piecemeal, plaintiff-by-plaintiff compliance. Given the Citizenship Clause backdrop and the risk that narrower relief would invite unequal treatment of similarly situated newborns across jurisdictions, procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against narrowing on an emergency stay posture without a merits determination. While Rule 23 may sometimes be the better vehicle, equity does not categorically bar broader injunctions when necessary to fully remedy the plaintiffs’ injury and prevent ongoing constitutional violations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may issue (and the Supreme Court should partially stay) “universal” injunctions that bar the Executive Branch from enforcing a presidential order against nonparties nationwide, even if relief to the named plaintiffs could be provided with narrower injunctions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing and judicial power); equitable remedial authority of federal courts (scope of injunctions); U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Citizenship Clause: “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof…”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Government (Trump, et al.) argues it is likely to succeed on the claim that the district courts’ injunctions are overbroad because universal injunctions exceed traditional equitable limits and are not justified merely by an assertedly unlawful policy; respondents allegedly cannot justify extending relief to nonparties, certain state respondents purportedly lack Article III standing, and the injunctions improperly interfere with internal Executive Branch operations. The Government also stresses that universal injunctions create practical and institutional harms: they incentivize avoidance of Rule 23 class certification, can impose relief on bystanders who may oppose it, and operate asymmetrically by preventing enforcement against anyone unless the government ‘runs the table’ in litigation everywhere. The Government seeks a partial stay narrowing the injunctions’ scope without requiring the Court to reach the underlying merits of the Citizenship Clause/birthright-citizenship dispute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents and supporting amici contend nationwide/universal relief can be necessary to provide complete relief in practice—especially in immigration/citizenship contexts where policy effects are not neatly confined to named plaintiffs and where piecemeal injunctions would be ineffective or unadministrable. They argue universal injunctions are not categorically barred by Article III and can be consistent with historical equitable practice and modern remedial schemes, pointing out that Congress has authorized broadly preclusive remedies in administrative law (e.g., APA “set aside” relief) and that the Court has tolerated broad remedial orders in prior cases. They also argue the Government is attempting to use the procedural posture (seeking narrowing without merits review) to undermine judicial checks on unlawful executive action, particularly where the challenged conduct is alleged to be unconstitutional, and they dispute the Government’s contention that the case is an ideal vehicle to constrain universal injunctions.
key_precedents: United States v. Wong Kim Ark, 169 U.S. 649 (1898)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—echoed by Justice Jackson—is that, in a uniform citizenship regime, plaintiff-only relief may be practically ineffective because administrative spillovers and unequal treatment could loop back and injure the plaintiffs. But under Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford, that argument must be shown as necessity to afford complete relief to these plaintiffs, not as a general preference for nationwide uniformity; on this record the injunctions have not demonstrated that narrower, plaintiff-protective relief (or relief tied to identifiable plaintiff interfaces) is unworkable. Justice Thomas’s Grupo Mexicano constraint reinforces my minimalism: absent class certification or statutory authorization, we should not extend equity into a default, nonparty-protective nationwide decree, and Sullivan v. Zebley’s class posture cuts the other way by highlighting Rule 23’s safeguards. I therefore would grant a partial stay narrowing the injunctions to plaintiffs (and any certified class) without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits, leaving respondents free to pursue class relief if administrability truly requires it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest argument—that plaintiff-only relief is practically ineffective because systemwide spillover harms and administrative chaos will continue to injure the plaintiffs—still treats administrative convenience as a source of remedial authority rather than a reason to use the proper procedural vehicle. Under an original public meaning of Article III and the historically bounded equitable tradition I referenced (consistent with Grupo Mexicano), a federal court’s injunction must be tethered to redressing the parties’ injuries; concerns about multiplicity or uniform administration do not license decrees for the benefit of strangers absent class certification or statutory authorization. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford reinforces that even when broader tailoring may sometimes be needed to secure “complete relief,” the relevant inquiry is necessity to protect the plaintiffs—not to regulate a program nationwide for nonparties. And to the extent Justice Sotomayor invokes Madsen or Sullivan v. Zebley, those precedents do not undermine my view because Sullivan’s breadth flowed through classwide relief with Rule 23 safeguards, which highlights the bypass problem rather than validating nonclass universal injunctions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s administrability and spillover-harm point is the most serious, but it still treats the desirability of a uniform nationwide rule as a substitute for the Article III requirement that relief be no more burdensome than necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries. As Chief Justice Roberts explains via Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford, the operative question is whether plaintiff-specific relief is genuinely inadequate to protect these plaintiffs—not whether broader relief would be cleaner for the Government’s programmatic administration. Justice Jackson’s invocation of historical equity tools to prevent multiplicity does not overcome Grupo Mexicano’s caution against expanding equity absent established practice; whatever “bills of peace” might show, they point toward structured representative litigation (Rule 23) rather than a default power to bind the Government as to strangers. Because Sullivan v. Zebley’s breadth rested on a certified class with procedural safeguards, it reinforces my view that universal injunctions here improperly mimic classwide relief without the prerequisites.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly stress Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford’s tailoring principle, but their framing assumes plaintiff-only relief will in fact deliver “complete relief” in a uniform, nationwide citizenship regime—an assumption respondents plausibly contest on this record because inconsistent recognition of citizenship status can predictably spill back onto plaintiffs through administrative interfaces and unequal treatment. Justice Thomas’s Grupo Mexicano point is the most serious constraint, yet even historically bounded equity asked whether narrower decrees would be practically ineffective or invite unadministrable multiplicity; the question here is necessity to prevent ongoing irreparable harm while merits are litigated, not whether Rule 23 is always the exclusive path to broader interim relief. Sullivan v. Zebley’s class posture does limit its force as direct authority for nonclass breadth, but it still underscores that when a federal rule operates uniformly, effective relief often must operate at the same level to avoid chaos and denial of rights in practice. Given the Government seeks scope-narrowing without addressing the substantial constitutional question, I would not partially stay relief in a way that risks continued, potentially unconstitutional burdens on vulnerable families during litigation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: in a uniform federal citizenship regime, party-only relief can be practically ineffective because administrative spillovers and unequal treatment can cycle back and injure the plaintiffs, making broader relief arguably “necessary.” But under the tailoring principle the Chief Justice invokes from Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford, the question is not whether nationwide uniformity is desirable but whether binding the Government as to nonparties is required to fully redress these plaintiffs—and the present record has not shown that plaintiff-protective relief (including relief covering their newborn children and state administrative interfaces) is unworkable. Sullivan v. Zebley, as Roberts and Barrett note, cuts against respondents’ position because its breadth was justified through a certified class, underscoring that when truly systemwide protection is needed, Rule 23 supplies the legitimacy and safeguards rather than defaulting to a universal injunction. Grupo Mexicano (Thomas) reinforces my pragmatic textualist bottom line: equity is flexible, but not a roving license to enlarge remedies beyond the parties absent a demonstrated necessity tied to plaintiffs’ injuries or a procedurally proper class vehicle.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s administrability and spillover argument is the strongest counter: in a uniform citizenship regime, inconsistent treatment of nonparties might create practical chaos that could indirectly affect plaintiffs. But as the Chief Justice explains, Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford set the controlling principle that equitable relief must be no more burdensome than necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ injury in fact; predicted disruption to program administration for nonparties cannot itself expand Article III’s judicial power or the traditional bounds of equity. Justice Thomas’s Grupo Mexicano point reinforces that we should be wary of treating universal injunctions as a default modern innovation untethered from historical practice, especially where Rule 23 offers a lawful mechanism (with safeguards) for broader relief when truly necessary. Nothing in Justice Jackson’s multiplicity concerns shows that plaintiff-protective relief (or class relief if certified) is unworkable here, so a partial stay narrowing the injunctions remains the sound course.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make their strongest point on administrability—spillover harms and chaos from a uniform citizenship policy may, as a practical matter, affect plaintiffs even if relief is formally limited to them. But under Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford, as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the relevant question is whether broader, nonparty relief is necessary to provide complete relief to the parties, and the current injunctions do not make that necessity showing; uniformity concerns alone do not enlarge Article III remedial power or equity beyond traditional limits. Sotomayor’s reliance on Sullivan v. Zebley does not undermine that conclusion because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett note, Sullivan’s breadth was anchored in a certified class with Rule 23 safeguards rather than a default power to issue universal injunctions. Consistent with Grupo Mexicano’s warning against equitable innovation, I would partially stay the injunctions as to nonparties while leaving plaintiffs free to seek broader relief through class certification or other procedurally proper mechanisms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best case that plaintiff-only relief can be practically ineffective in a uniform citizenship regime because spillover administrative chaos may itself injure the plaintiffs, potentially making broader relief "necessary" in an equity sense. But under Califano v. Yamasaki and Gill v. Whitford, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the dispositive inquiry remains whether broader relief is required to afford complete relief to these plaintiffs; generalized uniformity and equal-treatment concerns cannot by themselves expand the Article III “judicial Power” to bind the Government as to strangers absent class procedures. The invocation of Sullivan v. Zebley does not undermine that conclusion because, as Justice Kagan notes, its breadth was mediated through a certified class and Rule 23 safeguards—supporting the proposition that systemwide relief should ordinarily proceed via class certification rather than a universal injunction in an individual suit. Given Grupo Mexicano’s caution against equitable innovation untethered from historical practice, I remain persuaded a partial stay narrowing the injunctions to plaintiffs (and any certified class) is appropriate without reaching the Citizenship Clause merits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Califano v. Yamasaki/Gill v. Whitford framing is right about tailoring, but it assumes “complete relief” can be cleanly cabined to named parties when the Government is applying a single, uniform citizenship rule that predictably generates spillover and inconsistent status determinations that can continue to injure plaintiffs in practice. Justice Kagan’s contention that respondents have not shown plaintiff-only relief is unworkable is the closest call for me, yet at the stay posture the Government is asking us to narrow relief without squarely accounting for the real-world administrability and equal-treatment consequences that are integral to whether plaintiffs are actually protected pending merits review. Justice Thomas’s Grupo Mexicano point properly cautions against freewheeling equitable innovation, but historical equity’s concern with preventing multiplicity and avoiding chaotic, ineffective relief in the face of a unitary policy makes this a necessity-based question, not a categorical Rule 23-or-nothing rule. Because narrowing now risks practical ineffectiveness and procedural unfairness while the legality of the rule remains unresolved, I would deny the partial stay and leave the district court’s broader interim remedy in place for the moment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III limits the federal courts’ remedial power to resolving the case or controversy before them, and equitable relief should be tailored to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries rather than to regulate the Executive’s conduct toward nonparties nationwide. Our precedents caution that “injunctive relief should be no more burdensome to the defendant than necessary to provide complete relief to the plaintiffs,” Califano v. Yamasaki, 442 U.S. 682, 702 (1979), and that relief must be “limited to the inadequacy that produced the injury in fact,” Gill v. Whitford, 585 U.S. 48, 68 (2018). Where narrower relief can fully protect the named plaintiffs, a universal injunction extending to strangers to the suit departs from traditional equitable limits and risks institutional harms by effectively deciding nationwide policy without the procedural safeguards of class certification. I would therefore partially stay the injunctions to the extent they bar enforcement against nonparties, without reaching the underlying Citizenship Clause merits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III vests federal courts with the “judicial Power” to decide concrete cases and controversies, and that power traditionally permits equitable relief only so far as necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries, not to supervise the Executive’s enforcement against nonparties nationwide. Under the Founding-era equitable tradition incorporated by the Judiciary Act of 1789, the scope of remedies is constrained by historical equity practice; as we recognized in Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., federal courts may not expand equitable authority beyond what was traditionally exercised in English Chancery. Whatever occasional historical devices (e.g., bills of peace) existed to prevent multiplicity of suits, they do not justify modern “universal” injunctions where narrower relief to the named plaintiffs is feasible and where Rule 23 provides the proper mechanism for binding relief as to absent persons. Because these injunctions exceed traditional equitable limits and risk transforming Article III courts into roving commissions over executive policy, I would grant the Government’s request to partially stay and narrow them without reaching the merits of the Citizenship Clause dispute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III authorizes federal courts to resolve concrete disputes and award relief that is necessary to redress the injuries of the parties before the court; an injunction that bars enforcement against nonparties nationwide goes beyond what is required to provide complete relief to named plaintiffs and risks converting the Judiciary into a general supervisor of Executive policy. Whatever the ultimate merits of the Citizenship Clause question under the Fourteenth Amendment, the Government is likely to succeed in showing that these universal injunctions exceed traditional equitable limits and should be narrowed to the plaintiffs (or to properly certified classes), particularly given the serious practical consequences of universal relief—forum shopping, asymmetric nationwide paralysis of federal law, and circumvention of Rule 23’s safeguards. The Court has repeatedly signaled concern with overbroad injunctions and has narrowed such relief in emergency posture, see U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs v. N. Plains Res. Council, 141 S. Ct. 190 (2020) (mem.), and Justice Thomas’s concurrence in Trump v. Hawaii, 138 S. Ct. 2392, 2424–29 (2018) (Thomas, J., concurring), underscores that universal injunctions lack firm grounding in historical equity. Because narrower relief can protect the plaintiffs without disabling enforcement against everyone else, a partial stay is warranted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III and traditional equity do not impose a categorical bar on broader injunctive relief where narrower, plaintiff-only relief would be ineffective or unadministrable in practice, particularly in the citizenship/immigration context where a single federal policy operates nationwide and would predictably inflict ongoing harm on vulnerable populations. Under Madsen v. Women’s Health Ctr., an injunction must be no more burdensome than necessary to provide complete relief, but “complete relief” can require systemwide relief when the challenged policy’s uniform application would otherwise continue to injure the plaintiffs through spillover effects and administrative chaos. This Court has affirmed broad, nationwide remedial orders when necessary to remedy an unlawful regulatory scheme, as in Sullivan v. Zebley, and the Government’s request to narrow relief without confronting the serious constitutional question under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause risks insulating potentially unconstitutional executive action from meaningful judicial review. Given the practical consequences—uncertainty over citizenship status and attendant access to basic rights—equity favors maintaining relief sufficient to prevent ongoing, irreparable harm while litigation proceeds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III and traditional equity generally require remedies to be tailored to providing complete relief to the plaintiffs before the court, and the Government is likely right that sweeping relief for nonparties is hard to justify where narrower plaintiff-protective injunctions are workable. Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc. emphasizes that federal equitable authority is bounded by historical equitable practice, which cuts against treating “universal” injunctions as the default remedial form absent a class action or a statute expressly authorizing broadly preclusive relief. While respondents invoke administrability and the practical realities of citizenship/immigration policy, those considerations go to when broader relief may be necessary—not to a categorical entitlement to nationwide nonparty relief where complete plaintiff relief can be achieved more narrowly. Given the Government seeks only a partial stay narrowing scope without resolving the Fourteenth Amendment merits, a limited narrowing best reconciles equitable limits and workability while preserving respondents’ ability to obtain full relief for the parties with standing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III authorizes federal courts to resolve the cases of the parties before them, not to exercise a roving commission to supervise the Executive by enjoining enforcement against nonparties nationwide; equitable relief should be no broader than necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ own injuries. Our decision in Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo v. Alliance Bond Fund cautions that federal courts’ equitable powers are bounded by traditional limits and are not an invitation to innovate remedies untethered from historical practice, especially where narrower plaintiff-protective injunctions can provide complete relief. Whatever the merits of the Citizenship Clause claim under the Fourteenth Amendment, the Government is likely to succeed that the district courts’ universal injunctions exceed the judicial power and trench on separation-of-powers principles by effectively dictating executive policy for all persons everywhere. A partial stay narrowing relief to the named plaintiffs (and any properly established class) respects Article III limits while leaving respondents free to seek broader relief through Rule 23 or additional suits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III and traditional equitable principles generally require remedies to be tailored to redress the plaintiffs’ injuries rather than to regulate the Executive’s conduct as to nonparties nationwide, and a universal injunction often exceeds what is necessary to provide complete relief. Consistent with Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., federal courts’ equitable authority is constrained by historical practice and does not presumptively include sweeping, nonparty-protective injunctions absent clear authorization. Universal injunctions also create serious practical and institutional problems—forum shopping, avoidance of Rule 23, and nationwide policy paralysis from a single district court order—counseling a partial stay narrowing relief to the parties before the court. Without resolving the merits of the Citizenship Clause dispute, the injunctions should be limited to the minimum scope needed to remedy the named plaintiffs’ injuries.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III authorizes federal courts to resolve the parties’ case or controversy, and equitable relief must be limited to what is necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ injuries rather than to regulate the Executive’s conduct toward nonparties nationwide. Under Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., the scope of federal equitable power is constrained by traditional equitable practice, which generally tied injunctions to the protection of the litigants before the court, not the issuance of universal decrees absent classwide procedures. To the extent respondents invoke administrability concerns or the need for uniformity in citizenship/immigration contexts, those are policy arguments that do not expand Article III judicial power and are better addressed through tailored injunctions or Rule 23 class relief. Because narrower injunctions can provide complete relief to named plaintiffs without binding the Government as to nonparties, a partial stay narrowing the injunctions is warranted without reaching the merits of the Citizenship Clause dispute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III requires standing and limits relief to what is necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ injuries, but it does not categorically forbid broader equitable relief when narrower orders would be practically ineffective or unadministrable—particularly where a federal citizenship rule would otherwise operate inconsistently across jurisdictions and people similarly situated. Given the asserted constitutional conflict with the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and the systemic, nationwide operation of the challenged Executive policy, a nationwide injunction can be within traditional equitable authority to afford complete relief and preserve equal treatment pending merits review. The Government’s request for a partial stay that narrows relief without engaging the underlying constitutional merits risks undermining procedural fairness by leaving many identically situated persons exposed to an allegedly unconstitutional regime and forcing repetitive litigation. As Sullivan v. Zebley illustrates, systemwide relief (there via a nationwide class) is sometimes necessary to remedy a uniform federal policy, and channeling challenges into Rule 23 would not cure the Government’s asserted “asymmetry” concerns.
